reading_text: The birch at the edge of the yard leafs out before all the rest, green already while the ground is still cold underfoot. What began in that house was set down early, in leaner soil than anyone chose. Now the meltwater runs off the eaves and gathers in the low ground by the door, finding its own way down without being told. What moves through the rooms these days does not answer to plans, it follows its own slope. Keep to the way the water runs and you come to the old ground under the birch, the part of the place that stays yours whether you hold every stone of it or let some go. Would keeping all of it, or loosening your grip on some, sit easier with you as you look at that ground?

Before the water runs, there is only the slope and the rain that has not yet fallen — nothing carved, no channel worn, the ground open to any line the flow might take. Now the water moves, Anna, finding the low places by feel, gathering where the ground gives way and slowing where it holds. It does not consult a map, it reads the land under it as it goes. Keep letting it move this way and it wears its own bed into the hillside, a course that looks, in time, as though it were always meant to be there. The work ahead follows the same downhill logic, one turn opening onto the next. You stand at the top of the slope, watching the first thread of water pick its way down.

What was given in that house, Anna, was given fairly, hand meeting hand, the warmth passing both ways across the threshold. That balance was real, and it held for as long as it held. Something took root there that has not finished growing, carried out with you when you left, still quietly working in the dark like a seed under the floorboards. The friction is this: it wants ground you have not yet given it, and the old house is no longer that ground. The keys still lie in your palm, cool and familiar, though the lock they fit turns for someone else now. The house stays the house whether you hold them or set them down.

You set out along this road already sheltered, walled on one side by the river that has run here longer than any question you carry. That much was settled before you took a single step. Now the road runs past the old house of everything handed down to you, and the hardest part is that the path does not go through the door — it keeps to the water, leaving some of what is yours behind on the bank. That parting is not clean, and it is not meant to be comfortable. Ahead the track bends with the river and disappears around the next rise, out of sight but not out of reach. Keep to this pace and the road carries you on, one bend at a time, the water always to your left.

Long before you came to this fork, a seed was set in the ground beneath the scree, waiting through seasons for weight enough to crack it open. That waiting is done, and cannot be undone. Now the light comes up over the ridge and shows you the two tracks clearly, one going up the slope, one going down toward the water. Both are visible in this morning grey, and neither is closed to you yet. The scree holds its shape through every storm that batters it, moving stone by stone and never all at once. Walk on as you are and you become that slope — slow to shift, but shifting all the same, stronger for the wind that has worked you.

There was a voice, Anna, that spoke over what hurt in you and named it aloud, and that naming is set now, it cannot be taken back. Now the line runs down off the edge of the boat and into dark water, and nothing has touched it yet. Below the surface is only water you cannot see into, still being made as you watch. Where you are heading, the water narrows to a gate, and the mending you want waits on the far side of a thorn that will ask something of you first. Are you holding the line still because the water is deep, or because you are not yet ready to feel what takes it?

The iron lay cold and waiting in the dark of the shed, unmoved, holding the shape it was given long before you came to it. Now the coals are breathing and the metal begins to soften, warm enough at last to be worked, its old edges giving under the weight of the hammer. The forge throws its light across the walls and the iron glows from within, taking the form your hands are drawing out of it. Keep the fire fed and the shape goes on coming. What is worked while it is hot holds the mark of the hand that struck it.

There was a crossing you did not think you could make, and yet the horse beneath you found the ford, feeling the firm ground under the grey water where your eyes saw none. You trusted the steady thing carrying you more than you trusted the map, and that trust brought you to the far bank whole. Now the water still runs high with everything the ice let go this spring, and your strength is not a fixed hoard but a herd that moves, grazing and gathering as it goes. What you have to spend on your own mending is real, and it is on the move rather than locked away. Keep walking as you are, and the far shore turns out to be older ground than you knew, the home you carry rather than the one you left. The horse stands quiet in the pasture now, and the river runs on without you.
